shots.narration: Under Antarctica's ice there are lakes, volcanoes
and things that are alive.
Scientists reach them by melting holes straight down.
Doug is on the rope.
Doug did not agree to this.
Thin ice.
Blood Falls.
In the McMurdo Dry Valleys, a white glacier called Taylor Glacier
has a dark red stain pouring down its face, about five storeys high.
Here's the strange part.
It isn't blood.
The liquid comes out of the glacier perfectly clear, packed with dissolved iron,
and the moment it touches the air, that iron rusts,
like an old nail left out in the rain.
It isn't new, either.
The water was sealed under the glacier an estimated one and a half to two million years ago,
under about four hundred meters of ice, with no sunlight and no oxygen.
It is at least twice as salty as seawater, so it never freezes,
and in twenty fifteen a helicopter survey traced it at least twelve kilometers inland.
And it isn't empty.
Microbes live in it, breathing iron and sulfur instead of oxygen,
alone in the dark, the entire time.
The last time Doug was in Antarctica, he stood on top of it.
This time he took a selfie at the edge,
and the glacier front joined the photo.
Doug has died. Again.
The microbes have lasted more than a million years under that glacier,
and Doug lasted one selfie.
Erebus Ice Caves.
Mount Erebus is Earth's southernmost active volcano, almost three thousand eight hundred meters tall,
and at the top it keeps a lake of lava that stays there, year after year.
Every so often, a giant gas bubble bursts through it
and throws molten rock up to two hundred and fifty meters.
On its slopes, hot volcanic gas leaks out through cracks in the ground
and melts tunnels and caverns into the ice from below.
Where the steam reaches the surface, it freezes into hollow ice chimneys
that stand on the snow like smokestacks.
Some of the caverns are up to about twenty-five meters tall,
and the only way in is on a rope.
Outside, during one expedition, the air sat at about minus twenty-five degrees Celsius.
The catch is what happens inside.
Some of these caves get up to about twenty-five degrees Celsius,
warm enough, as one researcher put it, to be comfortable in a T-shirt.
So the warmest room on this trip is not on the ice.
It's inside it, on a volcano.
And something has already moved in.
Microbes live in these caves,
and in twenty seventeen, scientists sequenced DNA from the cave soil
and found traces of mosses, algae and small animals.
The researchers were careful about it.
DNA is not proof that anything is alive in there.
It's only proof that something was.
Doug took his jacket off, folded it into a pillow,
and lay down on the warm floor for a nap.
Doug is fine.
The air in volcanic caves is often the dangerous part.
Nobody should ever trust a cave this comfortable.
Thwaites From Below.
Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica has a nickname in the media.
They call it the Doomsday Glacier.
In twenty nineteen, airborne radar found a cavity growing under part of it,
covering about two thirds of the area of Manhattan.
It stood nearly three hundred meters tall, almost the height of the Eiffel Tower.
That space had once held about fourteen billion tons of ice,
and most of it had melted in only about three years.
So in twenty twenty, a team melted a hole straight through five hundred and eighty-seven meters of floating ice at Thwaites
and lowered a long, narrow robot called Icefin into the dark water underneath.
One of the scientists said that until then, nobody had data from the grounding line of any major glacier.
The worst part is what it saw on the underside.
The bottom of the ice was not smooth at all.
It was carved into steps and slots,
with crevasses tens of meters deep cut upward into it,
and warmer, saltier water was flowing into those slots and melting their walls sideways.
The flat parts were melting slowly.
The steep parts were melting fast,
and although they make up only about a tenth of the underside,
they were responsible for more than a quarter of the melting.
The glacier is being eaten from underneath, where nobody can see it, one crevasse at a time.
Doug swam into a crevasse with a torch to get a closer look at the ceiling.
The ceiling got a closer look at Doug.
According to NASA scientists, Thwaites holds enough ice to raise the world's oceans by about sixty-five centimeters.
The Fish Under the Ice.
In January twenty fifteen, a team in West Antarctica melted a hole through about seven hundred and forty meters of ice.
That's more than two Eiffel Towers stacked on top of each other.
The spot was about eight hundred and fifty kilometers from the front edge of the ice shelf,
right where the ice stops resting on the ground and starts to float.
Underneath, there was a gap of seawater only about ten meters deep,
roughly the height of an Olympic high-diving platform.
The team sent a small camera robot down the hole to look at the seabed.
The water was around minus two degrees Celsius, and it was permanently dark.
Here's what nobody expected.
Something swam up to the camera.
Pale, see-through fish about twenty centimeters long hovered right in front of the lens,
along with swarms of small crustaceans called amphipods,
and reports said they seemed curious about it.
They were the farthest south that fish had ever been found.
The scientists drilled to the edge of the world, and something was already waiting at the camera.
The ice above this gap does not sit still, either.
Near the grounding line, where it starts to float, the ice flexes up and down with the tides.
Doug waved at a fish,
and the fish looked back, which Doug took as a yes.
Doug has died. Again.
Nobody yet knows exactly what feeds the fish down here, this far from sunlight.
Lake Whillans.
Antarctica has hundreds of lakes hidden under its ice,
and until twenty thirteen, nobody had cleanly sampled a single one.
That January, a team set up a hot-water drill over a lake called Whillans
and melted a hole through about eight hundred meters of ice.
The drill heated its water to about ninety degrees Celsius,
and it was built to keep the team's own germs from going down the hole with them.
The lake itself is not deep.
It is only about one point eight meters deep, about the height of a tall man,
but it spreads out over about fifty-two square kilometers.
But that's not the disturbing part.
Every sample came back full.
There were about one hundred and thirty thousand cells in every milliliter of water,
which is about as crowded as an ordinary lake or the ocean.
A teaspoon holds five milliliters,
so that's around six hundred and fifty thousand living cells in a single spoonful of water that hasn't seen the sun.
The team counted nearly four thousand different kinds of microbes in the water.
None of them use sunlight.
Many get their energy from chemicals like iron, nitrogen and sulfur, released as the moving ice grinds the rock beneath it.
The first lake ever properly sampled under the ice was not empty.
Nothing down here is empty.
Doug brought a sandwich and a fishing rod,
because as far as Doug is concerned, a lake is a lake.
Doug is fine.
The microbes eat rock and want nothing from him,
and nothing at the bottom of a lake has ever ignored Doug before.
The Sponge Boulder.
In twenty twenty-one, scientists from the British Antarctic Survey published something they had found completely by accident.
They had drilled through almost nine hundred meters of the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf to collect mud from the seabed.
Instead of mud, their equipment hit a rock,
sitting on the seabed more than twelve hundred meters down.
When they checked the camera footage,
the boulder was covered in animals,
including sponges and other creatures that spend their whole lives fixed to one spot.
The spot was about two hundred and sixty kilometers from the open sea, in total darkness,
in water around minus two point two degrees Celsius.
That's colder than the inside of a refrigerator, with no light, ever.
The unsettling part is how these animals eat.
Sponges cannot move, so they filter food out of the water drifting past,
and in the open ocean that food starts as algae growing in sunlight near the surface.
Here, the researchers estimated that the nearest sunlit water upstream is somewhere between six hundred and twenty-five and fifteen hundred kilometers away.
The lead scientist asked the obvious question himself.
What are they eating?
Nobody knows yet, and nobody knows how they got there or how long they have been there.
They hit a rock by accident, and it was alive.
Doug decided to live like the sponges,
so he sat very still next to the boulder with his mouth open and waited for food to drift by.
The sponges have had a lot more practice.
Thick ice.
Mercer Subglacial Lake.
In late December twenty eighteen, a team melted a hole through one thousand and eighty-seven meters of ice to reach a lake that nobody had ever sampled.
The hole was only about forty centimeters wide,
a little narrower than a basketball hoop,
and they kept it open for about ten days.
They brought up water and mud from the lake floor
and looked at it under a microscope, expecting microbes.
Here's the problem.
In the mud, they found the carcasses of tiny crustaceans, each smaller than a poppy seed,
and the body of a tardigrade, an eight-legged animal often called a water bear.
The lead scientist was so surprised that he assumed the samples had been contaminated,
so the team cleaned everything and sampled again.
More shells came up.
None of these animals were alive, and they did not belong there.
They appear to be land animals, the kind that live in ponds and streams.
One idea is that they lived in the Transantarctic Mountains during a warmer spell.
When the cold came back, they were washed down by water under the ice,
or dragged in by an advancing glacier.
One researcher estimated that they died thousands of years ago, not millions.
The animals in this lake are not alive, and nobody knows exactly how they got there.
Doug went down to take notes,
and halfway through his second page, the rope stopped being attached to anything.
Doug has died. Again.
He is now the largest thing in the lake that nobody can explain.
Volcanoes Under the Ice.
In twenty seventeen, a team at the University of Edinburgh went through radar maps of the ground under West Antarctica,
looking for one very specific shape, a cone.
The idea came from an undergraduate student.
They found ninety-one volcanoes nobody had known about.
Added to the ones already known, that made one hundred and thirty-eight volcanoes under the West Antarctic ice sheet,
roughly two kilometers below the surface.
They are strung along a rift that runs for about three thousand five hundred kilometers.
Twenty-nine of them are more than a kilometer tall.
The tallest is about three thousand eight hundred and fifty meters high, about the height of Mount Fuji,
and it is completely buried.
The team described the area as potentially one of the largest volcanic regions on Earth,
and one news report noted that only East Africa's rift has volcanoes packed this densely.
You can't see any of it from the surface.
Here's the twist.
Nobody knows how many of these volcanoes are still active.
Even a quiet one can warm the ice from below and melt it into water,
and the researchers suggested that if the ice above them thins, volcanic activity could increase.
Nobody can check that yet.
One of the largest volcanic regions on Earth might be the one nobody can see.
Doug found a warm patch on the ground under two kilometers of ice and lay down on it,
because it was the first warm thing he had felt in hours.
The warm patch was warm for a reason.
Lake Ellsworth.
Lake Ellsworth is about eleven kilometers long, sealed under three point two kilometers of ice,
which is more than seven Empire State Buildings stacked on top of each other.
It is about one hundred and fifty meters deep,
and it may have been cut off from the outside world for up to a million years.
In December twenty twelve, a British team set up camp above it and started melting a hole straight down.
The plan came with a deadline,
because a hole melted with hot water starts freezing shut as soon as the hot water stops.
Once they broke into the lake, they would have about twenty-four hours to take their samples before the hole closed.
They never got that far.
First, the boiler that heats the drilling water failed.
Then, about three hundred meters down, the team could not link the main hole to a second hole they needed to recycle the drilling water.
They kept trying for more than a day,
and by then the fuel was too low to finish, so the attempt was called off.
The disturbing part is the timing.
The lake had waited perhaps a million years for someone to arrive,
and the hole to it began closing the moment the crew turned the heat off.
Doug was about halfway down when the crew packed up.
Nobody told him, because nobody had told Doug about the plan to begin with.
Doug has died. Again.
The team's leader said a return would take three to four years, maybe five.
The lake is still down there, untouched, and the hole to it is gone.
The bottom.
Lake Vostok.
Lake Vostok is the largest of the hundreds of lakes hidden under Antarctica's ice.
It is about two hundred and thirty kilometers long and fifty kilometers wide,
roughly the size of Lake Ontario,
and about eight hundred meters deep in its southern basin.
It sits under almost three thousand eight hundred meters of ice,
kept at about minus three degrees Celsius by heat coming up from the Earth.
How long it has been sealed off depends on who you ask.
Estimates run from about fifteen million years to about twenty-five million.
A Russian team at Vostok Station drilled toward it,
and for about thirty years they kept the hole open with kerosene and antifreeze so it would not freeze shut.
Other scientists worried that whatever came down that hole might end up in a lake nobody had ever touched.
In February twenty twelve, at three thousand seven hundred and sixty-six meters, the drill finally broke through.
Here's the part nobody planned for.
When the drill touched the lake, the water did not wait to be sampled.
It rushed up the borehole on its own, pushing the drilling fluid ahead of it,
and then it froze inside the hole.
The Russian team said that was good news, because water moving up meant less chance of anything moving down.
Even so, one American expert warned that the frozen samples could be contaminated,
because the upper part of the hole had never been drilled cleanly.
Doug knocked on the bottom of the hole to see if anybody was home.
Somebody was.
For millions of years, nothing touched this lake, and the first thing it did when we arrived was come up the hole.
The Deepest Point on Land.
In twenty nineteen, a team led by the University of California, Irvine published a new map of the ground hidden under Antarctica's ice.
Under the Denman Glacier in East Antarctica, it showed a canyon filled with ice
whose floor sits more than three thousand five hundred meters below sea level.
The ice in this part of the glacier is more than four kilometers thick,
the thickest stack of ice above Doug on this whole trip.
That makes the canyon floor the deepest point on land anywhere on Earth.
Only the trenches at the bottom of the ocean go deeper.
It is about eight times lower than the shore of the Dead Sea,
which is the lowest land you can stand on in the open air.
Nobody has measured the bottom directly.
Radar could not see it, because echoes from the steep canyon walls kept drowning out the signal from the floor.
So the team worked it out from how much ice flows through the canyon,
and how deep the canyon must be to carry it all.
That makes it an estimate, and the best one anyone has.
That's the real problem with this place.
The glacier is moving,
and between nineteen ninety-six and twenty eighteen, the point where it lifts off the ground and floats retreated more than five kilometers.
On one side of the glacier, the ground slopes deeper as you go inland,
the kind of slope that makes a retreat easier to keep going.
The lowest ground on any continent is down here, under the ice, and part of it slopes the wrong way.
Doug planted a flag that said "Doug was here",
which stayed true for about four seconds.
Doug has died. Again.
He isn't at the end of the world.
He's at the bottom of it, and the bottom is moving.
More than four kilometers of ice, the lowest ground on any continent, and the only thing that came back up was the cap.
Doug deaths: one hundred and thirty-nine.
The suitcase still has room.
